topicContent.heading: You're not just here to check a box.
topicContent.body: Welcome to Easy Way Driving School's Texas 6-Hour Adult Driver Education course. You're not just here to check a box. In about six hours, you're going to walk away with something the state of Texas takes seriously: proof that you know how to drive safely, legally, and responsibly.

bullets: You'll go through 9 short modules covering everything Texas requires
Each one builds on the last — traffic laws, right-of-way, staying safe, staying legal
At the end, you'll take the same exam the DPS uses for their written test
Pass it here, and you can skip the written test at the DPS office entirely

topicContent.heading: A quick hello from your instructor

meta.caption: Real instructor, real local school — not a stock avatar.

topicContent.body: True or false — completing this course replaces the DPS written test.

meta.answer: Mostly true — passing the exam in Module 9 lets you skip the written test at DPS entirely.

topicContent.heading: New drivers get into more crashes.
topicContent.body: Not because of recklessness — because the instincts that come from time behind the wheel just aren't there yet.

topicContent.heading: The real gap between new and experienced drivers
topicContent.body: Drivers age 16-19 have a fatal crash rate of 4.8 per 100 million miles — over 3x the rate of drivers in their 30s-50s. (Source: NHTSA / IIHS, 2021)

topicContent.heading: Here's the full picture by age

meta.caption: Source: NHTSA / IIHS, 2021 data. Highlighted bars = new-driver age range.

topicContent.heading: That's exactly why this course exists.
topicContent.body: Every module from here on is built to close that gap — not by lecturing you, but by giving you the judgment that usually only comes with experience.

topicContent.heading: Driving is a privilege Texas extends to you.
topicContent.body: With real responsibilities attached. Every rule you're about to learn exists because someone's safety depends on you knowing it.

topicContent.heading: This isn't about memorizing rules.
topicContent.body: It's about becoming someone Texas can trust with a license. Keep that in mind as we go.

topicContent.heading: Getting licensed is a real process.
topicContent.body: Getting a license isn't just showing up with cash and a photo. For most first-time adult applicants (18 and up), the path is: complete this course, pass the vision and knowledge exams, complete the Impact Texas Drivers (ITD) course, then pass the driving exam — no separate learner permit stage the way minors go through.

bullets: Pass the vision and knowledge (written) exams, plus the Impact Texas Drivers (ITD) course

topicContent.heading: What's actually on your license
topicContent.body: Every Texas license carries specific info beyond your photo: a license class (A, B, C, or M), any restriction codes (like corrective lenses or an automatic-transmission-only restriction), and sometimes an endorsement — the most common one for non-commercial drivers is adding a Class M motorcycle endorsement to an existing license. Restriction codes and endorsements aren't optional extras; driving outside them is its own violation, separate from anything else.

topicContent.heading: The Texas Driving with Disabilities Program
topicContent.body: If communicating with a peace officer during a traffic stop could be a challenge for you, Texas lets you add a "Communication Impediment" notation to your license or ID. Your doctor completes form DL-101, which you present at a driver license office — the notation goes on the back of your card, the same way an organ-donor or corrective-lenses code would. You can also disclose a communication impediment when you register a vehicle (form VTR-216), which flags it in the state's law enforcement system so an officer knows before they even approach your window.

topicContent.heading: Registration and insurance
topicContent.body: As of January 1, 2025, Texas eliminated the annual safety inspection requirement for ordinary non-commercial vehicles before registration — you no longer need a passing inspection to register your car. Some counties still require an emissions test in its place, and commercial vehicles still have their own inspection requirements. New owners have 30 days to register a vehicle after buying it, through their county tax assessor-collector. Separately, the Texas Motor Vehicle Safety Responsibility Act requires you to carry at least $30,000 of coverage per injured or killed person, $60,000 per crash, and $25,000 in property damage — and to be able to show evidence of it to a law enforcement officer or another driver after a crash.

topicContent.heading: Suspensions and revocations
topicContent.body: Certain convictions trigger automatic suspension — DWI, intoxication manslaughter or assault, failure to stop and render aid, evading arrest, and driving while your license is already invalid, among others. DPS can also suspend a license administratively, without a court conviction: for repeated violations (four in 12 months, or seven in 24), for causing a serious crash, or through Administrative License Revocation (ALR) — which kicks in automatically if you fail a breath or blood test at 0.08 BAC or higher, or refuse the test entirely.
True or false: a license can only be suspended after a criminal conviction.

meta.answer: False. Administrative actions — like failing or refusing a breath/blood test (ALR), or racking up repeated violations — can suspend a license with no criminal conviction at all.

topicContent.heading: Right-of-way is given, not taken.
topicContent.body: Almost every serious intersection crash comes down to one thing: someone got right-of-way wrong. Here's the single most useful reframe: right-of-way is something the law grants or requires you to yield — never something to take by force of speed or size. If another driver fails to follow the rules, the safe move is still to yield to them rather than insist on what's technically yours.

topicContent.heading: Controlled vs. uncontrolled
topicContent.body: A controlled intersection has a signal or sign telling you what to do — obey it. An uncontrolled one has nothing: no stop sign, no light. That's exactly where most right-of-way confusion happens, so know the fallback rule: yield to whoever is already in the intersection or approaching from your right.

meta.caption: First to stop, first to go. If it's a tie, the driver on the right goes first.

topicContent.heading: Turning and entering traffic
topicContent.body: When you're turning left, you yield to any oncoming vehicle going straight through — a green light doesn't change that, since the straight-through driver still has priority over your turn. The same yield-first rule applies whenever you're entering a road from a private driveway, parking lot, or alley: stop before the sidewalk and let approaching traffic and pedestrians go first.

topicContent.heading: A few more patterns worth knowing

bullets: T-intersections: traffic on the through road generally has the right-of-way
Unequal lanes or different pavement: the road that looks "major" isn't always legally right — go by signage, not appearance
Controlled-access roads (like freeway ramps): entering traffic yields to traffic already on the road

topicContent.heading: Roundabouts work differently
topicContent.body: Modern roundabouts use yield signs instead of signals: slow down, yield to traffic already circling, enter when there's a safe gap, then exit right without changing lanes inside the circle. It's not just courtesy — a well-used roundabout cuts severe crashes at that intersection by about 80% compared to a traditional signaled one, because there are far fewer points where two vehicles' paths can actually cross.

topicContent.heading: Railroad crossings
topicContent.body: At a railroad crossing, the train always has the right-of-way — no exceptions, no judgment calls. If a crossing signal is active or a gate is down, stop and stay stopped until it's clear. Never stop on the tracks, even in traffic — if you're stuck, pull through rather than block the crossing.

topicContent.heading: Emergency vehicles
topicContent.body: Texas's Move Over/Slow Down law requires drivers to move over a lane (when safe) or slow down significantly for stopped emergency, tow, utility, and TxDOT vehicles with their lights on. If you can't change lanes, the specific rule is: slow to at least 20 mph under the posted limit on roads at 25 mph or higher, or below 5 mph on slower roads. This applies to police cars, fire trucks, ambulances, tow trucks, and highway maintenance vehicles alike.

topicContent.heading: Yielding to motorcyclists
topicContent.body: Motorcyclists get the exact same right-of-way protections as any other vehicle — no less. The most common car-motorcycle crash happens when a driver turns left in front of an oncoming rider, often because a motorcycle's smaller profile makes its distance and speed harder to judge at a glance. Take the extra half-second to look again before you turn.

topicContent.heading: Pedestrians and school buses
topicContent.body: A driver must yield to a pedestrian in a crosswalk, marked or unmarked — but Texas law isn't a blanket "pedestrians always win": pedestrians also have duties, like not stepping into traffic so suddenly a driver can't safely stop. Treat it as yield, don't assume, not as an unconditional right-of-way in every situation. A school bus with its stop arm extended means traffic in both directions must stop — this is one of the few right-of-way rules that overrides even a divided road, except where a physical median separates the lanes.
Two cars arrive at a 4-way stop at the same time. Who goes first?

meta.answer: The driver on the right goes first, when both arrive at the same time.

topicContent.heading: Signs are a language without words.
topicContent.body: Every sign, signal, and painted line is a driver talking to you without saying anything. Learn the underlying system — shapes and colors mean specific things — and you can read almost any sign correctly the first time you see it, even ones you've never memorized.

topicContent.heading: Shape and color as a system

meta.caption: Octagon = stop. Triangle = yield. Diamond = warning. Round = railroad. The shape tells you the category before you even read the words.

topicContent.heading: Regulatory vs. warning signs
topicContent.body: Regulatory signs (mostly white/red or white/black rectangles) tell you what the law requires — speed limits, no turns, one-way. Warning signs (yellow diamonds) tell you what's ahead — curves, crossings, merges. Confusing the two categories is a common new-driver mistake.

topicContent.heading: Signals, including the confusing ones
topicContent.body: A steady red means stop, full stop. A flashing red works like a stop sign — stop, then proceed when clear. A flashing yellow means slow down and proceed with caution, no full stop required. Mixing these two up is one of the most common signal mistakes.

topicContent.heading: Pavement markings
topicContent.body: Yellow lines separate opposite-direction traffic; white lines separate same-direction lanes. A solid line means don't cross (no passing); a dashed line means you may cross when safe. Double solid yellow means neither direction may pass.
What's the difference between a flashing red and a flashing yellow signal?

meta.answer: Flashing red = treat like a stop sign, full stop then proceed when clear. Flashing yellow = slow down and proceed with caution, no full stop required.

topicContent.heading: The small rules that prevent chaos.
topicContent.body: This module is a grab-bag of the rules that quietly keep traffic from becoming chaos: following distance, speed, signaling, merging, and passing. Small rules, but they're the ones you use every single mile you drive.

topicContent.heading: Following distance
topicContent.body: For speeds of 30 mph or under, keep at least a 2-second gap from the car ahead; above 30 mph, make it 4 seconds — the higher speed needs more room to react. Pick a fixed point ahead (a sign, a shadow, an overpass) and count from when the car ahead passes it to when you do. In rain, heavy traffic, or low visibility, add more time on top of that.

topicContent.heading: Speed: legal isn't always safe
topicContent.body: Driving exactly at the posted limit is always legal — except when conditions like fog, rain, or heavy traffic make that speed unsafe. Texas law expects you to adjust for conditions, not just the sign.

topicContent.heading: How far it actually takes to stop
topicContent.body: At 60 mph on dry pavement with good brakes, it takes about 303 feet — roughly a football field — to think, react, and brake to a stop. At 30 mph it's about 109 feet. Speed doesn't just raise impact force; it eats the distance you have to avoid the crash in the first place.

topicContent.heading: Signaling your intentions
topicContent.body: Turn signals (or hand signals if yours fail) are required any time you change lanes, turn, pull away from a curb, slow to stop, or enter or leave a highway. Signal continuously for at least 100 feet before you turn, and turn the signal back off once you're through — a signal left on by mistake tells everyone around you the wrong thing.

topicContent.heading: Passing and blind spots
topicContent.body: Every vehicle has blind spots your mirrors don't cover — most critically just behind and to each side. A quick shoulder check before changing lanes catches what your mirrors alone can miss.

topicContent.heading: Speed shrinks what you can see
topicContent.body: Your normal field of vision is 180 degrees or more standing still. At 60 mph, it narrows to roughly a fifth of that. The faster you go, the less of the road around you you're actually able to take in.

topicContent.heading: The actual speed limits
topicContent.body: Unless posted otherwise: 30 mph in an urban district, 15 mph in an alley, and — a Texas-specific one — 15 mph on beaches and county roads next to a public beach. Numbered Texas or U.S. highways outside city limits top out at 70 mph for passenger vehicles; unnumbered highways top out at 60. Some limited-access highways post as high as 75–85 mph. Whatever's actually posted always controls.

topicContent.heading: Street racing is a real charge
topicContent.body: Racing, drag racing, speed or acceleration contests, and even just trying to set your car's top-speed record on a public road are all illegal under Transportation Code §545.420 — not just reckless, but a specific criminal offense ranging from a Class B misdemeanor up to a second-degree felony depending on the outcome.

topicContent.heading: Headlights aren't just for seeing
topicContent.body: Texas law requires headlights on starting 30 minutes after sunset until 30 minutes before sunrise, or anytime you can't clearly see people or vehicles 1,000 feet ahead — rain, fog, or dust count. Switch to low beams within 500 feet of an oncoming car, or within 300 feet of one you're following, so you're not blinding the driver ahead of or facing you.

topicContent.heading: Entering and leaving a freeway
topicContent.body: Entering, you yield to traffic already on the highway, use the speed lane to match traffic speed, then merge — don't just ease in at a crawl. Once you're on, hold a steady speed and keep at least a 2-second gap (4 in bad weather). Move into the exit lane early; the more traffic, the sooner you should get over, since exit signs are typically posted about 1,000 yards ahead.

topicContent.heading: Fatigue and highway hypnosis
topicContent.body: Long, monotonous stretches of driving can induce a kind of trance — "highway hypnosis" — where attention drifts without the driver noticing. Stop every two hours or 100 miles, get out and move around, and keep shifting your eyes between near and far instead of fixing on one point ahead.

topicContent.heading: If your car breaks down or you lose control
topicContent.body: Breakdown: get off the pavement if you can, turn on your hazards (taillights at night), and get everyone out and away from traffic if the car won't move. Skid: ease off the gas — don't stab the brakes — and steer gently toward the direction the back of the car is sliding. Brake failure: pump the brakes, downshift, and apply the parking brake carefully. Blowout: don't brake hard; ease off the gas and steer straight until you can safely pull over.

topicContent.heading: Winter driving
topicContent.body: There's no safe fixed speed on ice or snow — slow down until you've felt out how much traction you actually have, and give yourself far more following distance than usual. Watch for ice on bridges and shaded spots even when the rest of the road looks clear, and remember chains or snow tires help you go, not necessarily stop or turn any faster than normal.

meta.caption: Reduced speed limits in work zones are enforced whether or not you see anyone working.

topicContent.body: True or false: fines for traffic violations are higher in a work zone when workers are present.

meta.answer: True — under Transportation Code §542.404, both the minimum and maximum fine are doubled when workers are present and the zone is properly posted with its speed limit.

topicContent.heading: The module with the highest stakes.
topicContent.body: The difference between a bad decision and a life-changing one often comes down to information in the next 40 minutes. This module doesn't try to scare you — it just makes sure you actually know the rules, the numbers, and the consequences before you're ever in a position to need them.

topicContent.heading: Legal intoxication in Texas
topicContent.body: Texas defines intoxication as a blood alcohol concentration (BAC) of 0.08 or more for anyone 21 and older — or, at any age, not having the normal use of your mental or physical faculties. That means you can be legally intoxicated below 0.08 too, if alcohol or drugs have visibly impaired you.

topicContent.heading: Zero Tolerance for minors
topicContent.body: Texas law does not allow any detectable amount of alcohol for a driver under 21 — not a limit, a flat zero. A minor doesn't need to be "intoxicated" under the adult standard to be charged; any measurable amount while driving is its own offense.

topicContent.heading: It's not just alcohol
topicContent.body: Marijuana measurably affects concentration, judgment, and the sensory skills driving depends on, even at typical social doses. Stimulants like amphetamines make you more alert short-term but less coordinated and more crash-prone. Tranquilizers, sedatives, and even many over-the-counter cold and allergy medications can cause the same drowsiness and slowed reactions as alcohol — read the label. Mixing any of these with alcohol multiplies the effect rather than just adding to it.

topicContent.heading: How alcohol affects driving
topicContent.body: Alcohol slows reaction time, narrows peripheral vision, and impairs judgment about risk — often before a driver feels impaired at all. That gap between feeling fine and actually being able to drive safely is exactly what makes drinking and driving so dangerous.

topicContent.heading: Penalties, in plain terms
topicContent.body: A first adult DWI conviction can mean up to $2,000 in fines and 72 hours to 180 days in jail, with your license suspended 90 days to a year. If the crash causes injury, the charge becomes Intoxication Assault (up to 10 years); if it causes death, Intoxication Manslaughter (up to 20 years) — both felonies with fines up to $10,000. Minors face their own escalating scale for Minor in Possession offenses, starting at a Class C misdemeanor and moving to a Class B by a third offense.

topicContent.heading: Open Container and Implied Consent
topicContent.body: Texas's Open Container law makes it illegal to have an open alcoholic beverage in the passenger area, even if the driver isn't drinking — a standalone offense punishable by up to a $500 fine. The Open Container Enhancement Law raises the stakes further: having an open container present during a DWI arrest increases the mandatory minimum jail time. Implied Consent means that by driving in Texas, you've already agreed to a breath or blood test if arrested for suspected intoxication — refusing doesn't avoid the consequences, it just triggers its own license suspension instead.

topicContent.heading: Administrative License Revocation
topicContent.body: Separate from any criminal DWI charge, DPS can suspend your license administratively — no trial required — the moment you fail a breath or blood test at 0.08 BAC or above, or refuse to take one. This is Administrative License Revocation (ALR), and it runs on its own timeline alongside whatever happens in court.
True or false: a driver can be charged with an open container violation even if they aren't the one drinking.

meta.answer: True — the law applies to an open container anywhere in the passenger area, regardless of who's drinking.

topicContent.heading: You're never the only one out there.
topicContent.body: This module is about everyone else on the road — pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists, and more — and what's expected of you around them, including in situations that call for quick, level-headed decisions.

topicContent.heading: Who shares the road
topicContent.body: Beyond other cars: pedestrians, cyclists, motorcyclists, farm equipment, horses and horse-drawn conveyances, light rail trains, and motor-assisted scooters — collectively called vulnerable roadway users because they have far less protection than you do in a crash. Light rail is quieter than most buses or cars, so stay alert near tracks even when you can't hear a train coming, and never stop or park on the rails.

meta.caption: Give a cyclist real room — not just a courtesy tap of the wheel.

topicContent.heading: Sharing the road with oversized vehicles
topicContent.body: Trucks and oversize or overweight vehicles take longer to stop, need a wider turning radius, and have bigger blind spots than a car. A rule of thumb: if you can't see the truck driver in their side mirror, they can't see you. Give trucks extra following distance, never cut into the space in front of one, and when passing, complete it in one smooth move rather than lingering alongside.

topicContent.heading: Good Samaritan Law and crash scenes
topicContent.body: If you're at or near a crash scene, Texas's Good Samaritan Law offers legal protection for those who render reasonable aid in good faith. You're not expected to be a medical professional — just to help without fear of being sued for trying.

topicContent.heading: Defensive driving, in practice
topicContent.body: Defensive driving isn't a slogan — it's assuming other drivers might make mistakes, and leaving yourself room and time to react when they do. It's the difference between reacting to a hazard and already having a plan for it.

topicContent.heading: If stopped by law enforcement
topicContent.body: Pull over safely and promptly, stay in the vehicle unless told otherwise, keep hands visible, and have your license, registration, and insurance ready. This isn't just etiquette — it's what keeps a routine stop routine.

topicContent.heading: Open truck beds and hauling cargo
topicContent.body: It's illegal to drive with anyone under 18 riding in an open truck bed or open flatbed trailer, with narrow exceptions like parades or farm-to-market work. Cargo has its own rules too: loose material like gravel or dirt has to be fully enclosed or covered so nothing blows or spills onto the road, and any trailer you're towing needs safety chains attached — not just a hitch — so it can't break free if the connection fails.

topicContent.heading: Aggressive driving
topicContent.body: Aggressive driving is a pattern — tailgating, weaving, brake-checking — not a single mistake. The best response if you encounter it is to avoid engaging: don't match the behavior, give them room, and let them go.

topicContent.heading: Carbon monoxide risk
topicContent.body: A running vehicle in an enclosed space (like a closed garage) can build dangerous carbon monoxide levels quickly and silently. Never let an engine idle in an enclosed space, even briefly, and never use a heater or A/C in a parked car with the windows sealed in a tight space.

topicContent.heading: The Texas Driving with Disabilities Program
topicContent.body: If communicating with a peace officer during a stop could be a challenge, Texas lets a driver add a "Communication Impediment" notation to their license (form DL-101, signed by a doctor) or flag it privately in the state's law enforcement system when registering a vehicle (form VTR-216) — either way, it alerts an officer to the situation before they even reach the window.

topicContent.heading: Driving through a work zone
topicContent.body: A work zone isn't just a speed limit sign — know how to actually get through one: watch for a flagger holding a STOP/SLOW paddle or directing traffic by hand, follow the temporary signs and lane shifts exactly as posted, and don't try to beat merging traffic to a lane closure. Under Transportation Code §542.404, both the minimum and maximum fine for certain qualifying traffic offenses are doubled in a work zone when workers are present and the zone is properly posted — a violation that's a $200 fine elsewhere can be $400 there.
What does the Good Samaritan Law protect?

meta.answer: Someone who renders reasonable aid in good faith at a crash scene, from legal liability for that assistance.

topicContent.heading: Every drive involves risk. The goal is seeing it coming.
topicContent.body: You can't eliminate risk on the road — but you can get much better at spotting it before it becomes a problem. This module also covers something that has nothing to do with driving skill and everything to do with awareness: recognizing human trafficking.

topicContent.heading: Risk categories
topicContent.body: Think of risk on a scale: controlled, low, moderate, complex. An empty parking lot is controlled risk. A busy downtown intersection at rush hour is complex risk. Recognizing which one you're in changes how much margin you should be leaving yourself.

topicContent.heading: Perceived risk vs. actual risk
topicContent.body: New drivers often misjudge risk in both directions — overestimating harmless situations while underestimating genuinely dangerous ones. Experience closes that gap; until it does, lean toward caution when you're not sure.

topicContent.heading: The biggest risk most drivers underestimate
topicContent.body: Distraction doesn't have to mean texting — it's anything that pulls your eyes, hands, or mind off driving: adjusting navigation or music, eating or drinking, personal grooming, digging for something in the car, or just a passenger — or pet — demanding attention. If a distraction slows your reaction time by even half a second, your odds of crashing roughly double.
True or false: it's legal to check a text at a red light, since the car isn't moving.

meta.answer: False — Texas law prohibits reading, writing, or sending an electronic message while operating a vehicle, which includes while stopped in traffic or at a light. The only exceptions are contacting emergency services or using a hands-free device.

topicContent.heading: Buckling up is still the single best odds-improver
topicContent.body: Every seat in the car — driver and passengers, front and back — is required to be belted if the vehicle has a belt for it. Being thrown from a vehicle in a crash makes death about five times more likely; a seat belt is what keeps that from happening. It does more for your survival odds than almost anything else on this list.

topicContent.heading: Why night driving carries more risk
topicContent.body: You see less at night — your headlights only light so far ahead, and other drivers, pedestrians, and animals are harder to spot until they're close. Fatigue is also more likely on top of reduced visibility. If a trip can be done in daylight instead, it's the lower-risk choice; if you must drive at night, slow down enough that you can stop within the distance your headlights actually light up.

topicContent.heading: Space management: Search, Evaluate, Execute
topicContent.body: SEE is a simple mental loop: Search the road ahead and around you, Evaluate what you find for risk, then Execute the safest response. Running this loop constantly — not just when something goes wrong — is what separates a defensive driver from someone who's just reacting.

topicContent.heading: Why new drivers are over-represented
topicContent.body: New drivers are involved in a disproportionate share of crashes, injuries, and fatalities — especially ones involving speed, alcohol, single-vehicle loss of control, and running off the road. It's not that new drivers are worse people; it's that the judgment gap takes real time behind the wheel to close.

topicContent.heading: Speed is a risk multiplier, not just a rule
topicContent.body: Higher speed means less time to react, a longer distance to stop, and a harder impact if you can't. It's also the difference between a legal risk and a criminal one — street racing, speed contests, or just trying to set a personal top-speed record on a public road is a specific offense under Texas law, not just reckless driving.

topicContent.heading: Recognizing human trafficking
topicContent.body: Watch for signs someone may be a trafficking victim: visible fear or anxiety around a controlling companion, avoiding eye contact or being unable to speak for themselves, signs of physical abuse, or someone who seems unable to come and go freely. If you notice these signs, don't intervene directly — call the National Human Trafficking Hotline at 1-888-373-7888 or text 233733, or call 911 if someone is in immediate danger.
What does the "E" in SEE stand for, and what does it mean in practice?

meta.answer: Evaluate — assessing what you've spotted while searching, for how much risk it actually presents, before deciding how to respond.
